title: Cucurbitacin B enhances cisplatin-induced cytotoxicity in osteosarcoma cell lines in vitro through a STAT3/MYLK4-associated HMGB1/NF-κB pathway
content:
Abstract
Cisplatin resistance is a major contributor to unsatisfactory therapeutic outcomes in osteosarcoma. Cucurbitacin B has been validated to exert anti-tumor activity and strengthen chemotherapeutic sensitivity in multiple malignancies, yet the detailed molecular cascade through which cucurbitacin B enhances the cytotoxic effect of cisplatin in parental osteosarcoma cells remains largely undefined. In this study, MTT and colony formation experiments were adopted to detect cell viability and proliferative capacity, while flow cytometry was utilized to quantify cell apoptosis. RT-qPCR and western blot were performed to detect the expression levels of target molecules, immunofluorescence staining visualized the subcellular distribution of HMGB1, co-immunoprecipitation verified the protein binding between MYLK4 and HMGB1, and ChIP combined with dual-luciferase reporter assays confirmed the transcriptional binding of STAT3 to the MYLK4 promoter. Functional results demonstrated that cucurbitacin B enhanced cisplatin-induced growth suppression and apoptosis in osteosarcoma cells. Mechanistically, cucurbitacin B suppressed STAT3 to reduce MYLK4 expression, which further blocked MYLK4-dependent HMGB1 phosphorylation, affected HMGB1 subcellular distribution, and ultimately inactivated the NF-κB signaling cascade. Rescue experiments revealed that overexpressing STAT3 or MYLK4 counteracted the chemosensitization of cucurbitacin B, whereas MYLK4 knockdown partially rescued the effects triggered by STAT3 upregulation. Collectively, cucurbitacin B enhances the cytotoxic effect of cisplatin in parental osteosarcoma cells by inhibiting the STAT3/MYLK4 signaling axis and interrupting HMGB1/NF-κB pathway activation. These findings support a role for STAT3/MYLK4-associated signaling in the enhanced cytotoxic effects of CuB/DDP in parental osteosarcoma cell lines in vitro.
